dataset.name: Research notes — multi-hop
dataset.description: Synthetic English reading notes following one replication dispute across eight months. Deliberately weighted to multi-hop and aggregation: most answers need two or three sessions, so a pipeline that retrieves one perfect chunk still scores badly. All authors, institutions and findings are fictional.

messages.content: Reading notes: the original 2014 study reported an effect size of 0.48, on 240 undergraduates at one university.
Noted. Worth checking what the confidence interval was before treating that as the reference value.
The replication: the 2019 replication found an effect size of 0.21, less than half the original. The interval excludes the original estimate.
So the disagreement is not just about power. That is the part the commentaries will focus on.
Scale of the replication: the replication used 1,842 participants across nine sites.
Nine sites is enough to look at between-site variation, which the original could not.
Funding note: the Vestrand Foundation funded both the original study and the replication. That answers the obvious objection about adversarial replication.
Then the funding argument cuts the other way from how it is usually used.
Methods comparison: both studies used the same 14-item attention scale, administered in the same order.
So an instrument difference cannot explain the gap.
Commentary: Ohlsson argues the replication changed the incentive structure of the task. His claim is that the payment schedule made the task easier to satisfice.
That is testable against the per-site data, if they released it.
Reply published: the replication authors answered that the incentive change was pre-registered and appears in the accepted protocol.
Then the objection is about whether the change was wise, not whether it was hidden.
Site-level detail: the Bergen site alone reported an effect size of 0.51, close to the original.
One site matching the original is what you would expect from sampling variation alone, so it is weak evidence on its own.
Also: three sites were excluded from the pooled estimate for protocol deviations. The pooled figure is over six sites, not nine.
That is worth stating whenever the 0.21 is quoted.
Attrition: dropout was 11% in the replication and 4% in the original.
Higher but not alarming, and it is in the direction the online format would predict.
Meta-analysis: the 2022 meta-analysis pooled 31 studies and reported 0.26, with substantial heterogeneity.
So the pooled estimate sits between the two, closer to the replication.
Context: pre-registration became a journal requirement in 2018, which is after the original and before the replication.
That explains why only one of the two has an accepted protocol to point at.
Instrumentation: all sites ran the task in the same open-source presentation software, version-pinned.
Then timing differences between sites are hardware, not software.
Draft argument: the original is the outlier, not the replication.
The meta-analytic estimate supports that reading, and the single-site match does not undercut it.
New evidence: a 2025 registered report with 4,100 participants reported 0.19, the largest sample so far.
That moves the pooled estimate down again and is hard to dismiss on power.
Reviewer question: how many participants in total across the replication and the 2025 registered report?
Add the two numbers reported in the notes rather than quoting either alone.
Decision: the review will report a range rather than a point estimate.
Given the heterogeneity that is the defensible choice.
Submitted. The funding and pre-registration notes are in the limitations section.
Good. Those are the two things a reader will otherwise ask about.
